"Where are we?" and "What should we do?" are two very different questions.

One asks for an update on the current situation. The other asks for help making a decision. Even when the project is the same, the document should reflect what the reader needs.

That's why Briefly supports different brief types: https://briefly.garrettsdevdesk.com

A good project status update should answer "Where are we right now?" without making someone read through an entire week of activity.

Focus on what changed, what matters, what's blocked, and what happens next. Those four pieces give the reader a useful picture of the project's current position.

Try that structure with your next weekly update.

When someone asks for an executive brief, they're usually looking for the important picture without having to reconstruct it from dozens of details.

Give them the context, key facts, risks, and direction they need to understand the situation quickly.

Briefly includes an executive brief format you can use: https://briefly.garrettsdevdesk.com

A decision brief should make the actual choice easy to understand.

What are the realistic options? What are the trade-offs? What could go wrong? Which direction do you recommend, and why?

If you're preparing a document to help someone make a decision, try answering those questions before worrying about formatting.

The same project might need a status update, an executive brief, and a decision brief in the same week.

The underlying facts haven't changed. The audience and the purpose have.

Choosing the right structure helps you present the information in a way that's useful to each reader.

Explore the different formats in Briefly: https://briefly.garrettsdevdesk.com

Before choosing a template for your next work update, ask what question the document needs to answer.

Where are we? What do I need to know? What should we do?

Once you understand the reader's question, choosing the right structure becomes much easier.

Which of those three documents do you find yourself writing most often?
